prize_parts.citation: for empirical analyses of how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: The China-shock papers pair a clear question with transparent, widely reusable research designs. They showed that adjustment to trade shocks is slow and costly for local labour markets, which contradicted the standard expectation of rapid reallocation. The findings have been re-examined many times, including through critiques of shift-share inference, and the core result of persistent local effects has largely survived. Autor's task-based work gives the technology side a coherent conceptual frame, so the trio addresses one question: how external shocks to labour demand reach workers and places. The scientific influence on trade, labour and public economics and on the policy debate on globalisation and automation is large. After reading colleagues' openings, I still rank this first among the shortlisted candidates, since it combines credible designs, a decade-plus of scrutiny and a clean attribution for the China-shock core (Autor, Dorn, Hanson).
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B023 bundles two strands, skill-biased and task-based technical change and the China trade shock. Their credit is entangled with work already recognised (Card, Goldin, Acemoglu), and the proposed trio omits Katz, who anchors the older wage-structure literature. The magnitude and persistence of the trade-shock effects, and the identification in shift-share designs, are still debated. The research-design principle I value, credible and transparent evidence, is better served by the China-shock strand than by the broader technology-and-inequality narrative, and a citation that claims both may overreach.

responses.point: Fredriksson also ranks B023 first and proposes Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that Autor and Katz anchor the technology, tasks and wage-structure line, that Hanson is central to the trade evidence, and that Katz's other contributions strengthen his case.
responses.response: I agree that the technology and trade strands together make the more significant scientific story, and that a three-name limit forces a hard choice. I still favour Dorn over Katz. The Autor-Dorn-Hanson papers are the unified, jointly authored core, with the same design and data. Katz's skill-premium work overlaps with the Goldin-Katz tradition already recognised in 2023, and his mobility work belongs to a different ballot (B031). Including Katz would make the citation wider but less sharp. If the committee wants the technology strand to be explicit, I would take that as a reason to widen the citation's wording, not as a reason to drop Dorn.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the Kiyotaki-Moore and Gertler financial-frictions work (B006) first as the standard way macro models credit and financial frictions. He ranks B023 third and calls the exclusion of Dorn in favour of Katz a close call, with credit partly overlapping prior recognition.
responses.response: I accept that B006 is conceptually foundational and mature, and I do not dismiss its theoretical weight. My reservation is evidential. Several colleagues, including Hassler, Stromberg and Hjalmarsson, note that identifying the collateral channel empirically is mixed, and that the accelerator lineage is partly absorbed by Bernanke's 2022 recognition. I weigh designs that have survived repeated re-analysis more heavily than a mechanism that is influential but hard to pin down. On the Dorn-versus-Katz point I share Krusell's sense that it is close. His own observation that the China-shock papers are Autor-Dorn-Hanson is what tips it for me.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first with a two-person Kiyotaki-Moore proposal, on the grounds that the attribution is cleanest and Gertler's accelerator work builds on Bernanke's already recognised contribution. He ranks B023 fourth, with Autor, Hanson and Dorn, citing an unclear credit boundary with Acemoglu, Restrepo and Katz and some contested findings.
responses.response: I agree that a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore award would be the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and it is a fair point against my own three-name B023. The boundary problem he raises for B023 is real, because the task-model theory sits partly with Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are outside the credited names. That is why I would anchor the citation in the empirical analysis of labour demand and local adjustment and not claim the task-model theory. On maturity I read the evidence differently. The China-shock core is now over a decade old, and its main result has persisted through the debates on shift-share inference and magnitudes.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B023 fifth. She notes that the bundle merges separate discoveries, that credit is split across skill-premium, tasks and China-shock lines, and that some China-shock magnitudes and mechanisms are contested.
responses.response: This is the most important qualification on my own preferred candidate, and I largely accept it. The proposed trio and citation are an attempt to reduce the problem by focusing on empirical evidence about shocks to labour demand and local adjustment, with Autor's work as the link between the two strands. If the committee judges that this still merges distinct discoveries, I would treat B003 (Mian and Sufi) as my fallback, since it has a tighter attribution, and not widen B023 further.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B047 first and proposes a two-person Autor-Hanson award on B023, ranked third. He regards that pair as the tightest attribution but acknowledges that it omits meaningful co-creators, such as Dorn and Katz, and that the trade-shock magnitudes are still debated.
responses.response: I agree with his concern about attribution but not with the cut. Dorn is a full co-author of the central China-shock papers and the underlying data work, so a two-person award for Autor and Hanson would omit a co-originator in order to get a smaller number. Since the three-person cap does not bind here, I would keep Dorn. I also note that Strömberg ranks B047 (BLP) first. It has a clear methodological core, but structural estimation depends on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions, and I give those somewhat less weight than designs whose identifying variation is transparent.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads B023 as one coherent discovery or as two strands (technology and tasks, and trade shocks) that should not share a citation.
Whether Dorn or Katz belongs in the third place. I rely on recall of the authorship patterns and have not independently verified the citation or contribution data.
How persistent and how large the local labour-market effects of the China shock are, and how robust the shift-share inference is.
How much thematic overlap with the 2021 (Card), 2023 (Goldin) and 2024 (Acemoglu) prizes should weigh against the candidate.
Whether B003 and B036 would gain support from members who see B023 as bundled or as overlapping prior prizes.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My listed co-authors and affiliations (Johannesson, Ellingsen, Brodeur and the Institute for Replication, Camerer, Rand, Nowak and others) are not credited names on any shortlisted ballot.
